name: Korea Digital Nomad Visa (F-1-D)
description: Everything about Korea's F-1-D Workation Visa: ₩88M income requirement, insurance, documents, step-by-step application, and FAQ. Updated for 2026.
keyRequirement: Remote employment with foreign company + income ≥ GNI×2 (~₩88M/year)
targetAudience: Remote workers employed by foreign companies
Digital professionals working across time zones

eligibility.label: Working remotely for foreign employer
eligibility.description: Employment must be with company outside Korea

eligibility.label: Health insurance with Korea coverage
eligibility.description: Private health insurance with minimum coverage of approximately ₩100,000,000. F-1-D holders are generally not eligible for Korea's National Health Insurance (국민건강보험) as workplace subscribers. Maintain private coverage for the entire duration of stay.
warnings: Must maintain valid health insurance throughout stay

eligibility.label: Not working for Korean companies
eligibility.description: Cannot work for Korean clients/companies on this visa
warnings: Working for Korean companies is a visa violation

fees.notes: Additional fees may apply at embassy

incomeRequirement.notes: Twice the previous year's GNI per capita as announced by the Bank of Korea (한국은행). Based on 2024 GNI of ₩44,051,000, currently ~₩88,102,000/year. Updated annually (typically April). USD equivalent depends on exchange rate at application date (~$64,000–66,000 at recent rates). Proof required for previous 6-12 months.
proofMethods: Pay stubs or salary statements from the past 6-12 months
Tax return or income tax certificate from home country
Bank statements showing regular income deposits
For freelancers: invoices and contracts totaling the required amount over the past 12 months

insuranceRequirement.notes: Published requirements specify private health insurance with minimum coverage of ₩100,000,000. F-1-D holders are generally not eligible for Korea's National Health Insurance (NHI) as they are not employed by a Korean entity. International plans such as SafetyWing, Cigna Global, and World Nomads are commonly used. Insurance must cover the entire duration of stay.

taxImplications.notes: According to Korean tax law, individuals who stay in Korea for 183 days or more in a calendar year may be classified as tax residents. Tax residents may be subject to Korean income tax on worldwide income. The tax rate is progressive (6-45%). Double tax treaties may apply depending on nationality. Consult a licensed tax professional (세무사) for specific guidance.

documents.name: Valid Passport
documents.description: Must be valid for at least 6 months beyond intended stay

documents.name: Proof of Remote Employment
documents.description: Employment contract or letter from employer confirming remote work arrangement
tips: Letter should state you work remotely
Include job title and employment duration

documents.name: Income Documentation
documents.description: Bank statements, tax returns, or pay stubs showing ₩88,000,000+ annual income

documents.name: Health Insurance Certificate
documents.description: Proof of health insurance valid in Korea
tips: SafetyWing, Cigna Global, and similar accepted

documents.name: Criminal Background Check
documents.description: Police clearance certificate from your home country

documents.name: Proof of Accommodation
documents.description: Hotel booking, lease agreement, or Airbnb reservation
tips: At least first 2 weeks of accommodation

applicationSteps.title: Check Eligibility
applicationSteps.description: Verify you meet income requirement (₩88,000,000+) and have remote work arrangement.

applicationSteps.title: Prepare Documents
applicationSteps.description: Collect all required documents. Get employer letter and income proof.

applicationSteps.title: Apply at Korean Embassy
applicationSteps.description: Submit application at Korean embassy/consulate in your country. Alternatively, if you are currently in Korea on a valid visa status (e.g., B-1, B-2, D-10), you may apply for a change of status at the local immigration office.

applicationSteps.title: Receive Visa & Enter Korea
applicationSteps.description: Pick up your visa and enter Korea.

applicationSteps.title: Register at Immigration
applicationSteps.description: Within 90 days of arrival, register at local immigration office to get ARC.

processingTime.notes: Processing times vary by embassy, nationality, and season. According to published guidelines, apply at least 4-6 weeks before your intended travel date. Some embassies may offer expedited processing for additional fees.

restrictions: Cannot be employed by Korean entities
workPermission.notes: This visa is specifically for remote work. Working for Korean clients requires different visa.

postArrivalSteps.title: Alien Registration Card (ARC)
postArrivalSteps.description: Visit your local immigration office to apply for ARC. Required for banking, phone contracts, and most services.
tips: Bring passport, photos, proof of address, and visa-specific documents

faqs.question: What counts as 'remote work' for this visa?
faqs.answer: You must be employed by or contracting with companies outside Korea. This includes remote employees, freelancers with foreign clients, and entrepreneurs with foreign-registered businesses.

faqs.question: Can I work for Korean clients on this visa?
faqs.answer: No. The F-1-D is specifically for work with foreign companies. Working for Korean clients requires different work authorization.

faqs.question: What if my income varies as a freelancer?
faqs.answer: You need to demonstrate average annual income of approximately ₩88,000,000 (GNI × 2). Provide 6-12 months of bank statements and invoices showing consistent income.

faqs.question: Can I bring my family?
faqs.answer: Yes, spouse and children can apply for dependent visas (F-3). They cannot work on dependent visas without separate authorization.

faqs.question: What health insurance is accepted?
faqs.answer: International health insurance plans covering Korea are accepted. Popular options include SafetyWing, Cigna Global, and Allianz. The policy must be valid for your entire stay.

faqs.question: Can I extend beyond 2 years?
faqs.answer: The maximum stay on F-1-D is 2 years. After that, you'd need to leave Korea or qualify for a different visa type.

faqs.question: What are the tax implications of staying in Korea on an F-1-D visa?
faqs.answer: According to Korean tax law, individuals who maintain a domicile in Korea or reside for 183 days or more during a tax year may be considered tax residents. Tax residents may be subject to Korean income tax on worldwide income. Tax treaty provisions between Korea and your home country may apply. Consult a licensed tax professional for specific guidance.

faqs.question: Can I switch from F-1-D to an employment visa (E-7)?
faqs.answer: According to published immigration guidelines, a change of visa status from F-1-D to E-7 is possible if you secure a job offer from a Korean company that meets E-7 sponsorship requirements. You would need to apply for a change of status at your local immigration office before the F-1-D expires. Note that E-7 requires working exclusively for the sponsoring Korean employer.

faqs.question: Can I start a business in Korea on an F-1-D visa?
faqs.answer: The F-1-D visa does not authorize business operations in Korea. To start a business, you would typically need to transition to a D-8 (Corporate Investment) visa, which requires a minimum investment of approximately ₩100,000,000 and a registered Korean business entity.

faqs.question: Is it possible to change status within Korea, or must I leave the country?
faqs.answer: According to published immigration procedures, change of visa status within Korea is generally possible at the local immigration office (출입국·외국인청). However, certain transitions may require exiting and re-entering Korea. Check with the Korea Immigration Service or HiKorea portal for current requirements.

faqs.question: How does the income requirement work for freelancers?
faqs.answer: Freelancers must demonstrate average annual income of approximately ₩88,000,000 (GNI × 2) from foreign clients. Published requirements indicate that acceptable proof includes: invoices and contracts from the previous 12 months, bank statements showing deposits, and tax returns from the home country. Income must be from work performed for entities outside of Korea.

faqs.question: Can my family accompany me to Korea?
faqs.answer: According to published requirements, spouses and children of F-1-D holders may apply for F-3 (dependent) visas. F-3 holders cannot work in Korea without separate work authorization. The dependent visa application requires proof of relationship (marriage certificate, birth certificates) and the primary visa holder's documentation.

faqs.question: What happens when my F-1-D visa expires after 2 years?
faqs.answer: The F-1-D visa has a published maximum duration of 2 years (1 year initial + 1 year extension). After expiration, holders must either leave Korea or transition to a different visa type. Published transition options include: E-7 (if employed by a Korean company), D-8 (if investing in a Korean business), or D-10 (job-seeking visa, if holding a bachelor's degree or higher).

tips: Apply well in advance - processing times vary by embassy
Keep detailed income records - you'll need them for extension
Get international health insurance before applying
Consider time zones - Korea is GMT+9
Join digital nomad communities in Seoul for networking
warnings: Income requirement is strict — approximately ₩88M based on GNI × 2

communityTips.tip: FBI background check can take 12-18 weeks via mail. Start this FIRST before anything else.
SafetyWing Nomad Insurance was accepted at Seoul Immigration Office for my F-1-D extension. Cost about ₩60,000/month.
I used Wise (TransferWise) bank statements + employment contract. They accepted it without issues at the Sejongno office.
Got my ARC card in 10 business days after registering at Mokdong immigration. They give you a receipt right away that works as temp ID.
If you're American, get your background check apostilled at the US State Department before coming. Takes 4-6 weeks by mail.

pathsTo.name: Professional Employment Visa
pathsTo.requirements: Secure a job offer from a Korean company. Must meet E-7 qualifications (bachelor's degree or 5+ years experience).
pathsTo.notes: For digital nomads who find local Korean employment. This means giving up remote work for foreign companies — a major lifestyle change. Korean employers must sponsor your visa. Verify current in-country change of status procedures with the local immigration office.

pathsTo.name: Corporate Investment Visa
pathsTo.requirements: Register a business in Korea with minimum investment of ~₩100,000,000. Must demonstrate viable business operations.
pathsTo.notes: For digital nomads who want to establish a Korean business entity. The investment threshold is significant. Some nomads transition by incorporating their existing remote business in Korea.

pathsTo.name: Job Seeking Visa
pathsTo.requirements: Must have bachelor's degree or higher. Apply before F-1-D expires (max 2 years).
pathsTo.notes: A bridge option if your F-1-D is expiring and you want to stay in Korea to find local employment. D-10 gives you up to 2 years to job search.

pathsFrom.name: Job Seeking Visa
pathsFrom.requirements: Remote employment with a foreign company and annual income of ₩88,000,000+ (GNI × 2). Must have health insurance covering Korea.
pathsFrom.notes: For D-10 holders who find remote work with foreign companies. The income requirement is strict (~₩88M/year). This is an alternative to seeking Korean employment.
